title: Making the Complex Simple Takes Talent
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Opening with Pascal's apology for writing a long letter for want of time to write a short one, this piece argues that simplification is a demanding intellectual act rather than a presentational one. Its causal claim is that clear explanation is downstream of genuine understanding, and that people who have not grasped an issue at its core are structurally unable to explain it in a way others can use. When real understanding is present, the essay says, complexity does not have to be fought off so much as it melts away and is replaced by something more elegant. Two concrete techniques are named: finding a story, metaphor or analogy that paints the core elements, and replacing jargon and technical terms with everyday language. The piece then turns pointed, observing that anyone can render a complex idea more complex, and reading deliberate obscurity as an attempt to project sophistication that fails. The closing standard is demanding and is addressed inward first, requiring more simplicity of oneself before requiring it of others.
points: The causal claim is the useful one: clarity of explanation is evidence of understanding, so an explanation others cannot use is a diagnostic about the explainer, not the audience.
Two techniques are named specifically, a fitting story, metaphor or analogy for the core elements, and the replacement of jargon and technical terms with everyday language.
Obscurity is read as a status move rather than a necessity, an attempt to project a sophisticated self-image that the piece says falls flat.
The asymmetry is stated plainly, that anyone can make a complex idea more complex, which is what makes simplification a genuine test of talent.
The standard is turned inward before it is turned outward: get your own thinking clear enough to make it simple for others.
quotes: Getting to simple is hard and takes real brain power. Simplifying the complex takes time and wisdom.
It requires true insight into the issue or problem, which is always in short supply, even among so-called experts.
Those who fail to understand an issue at its core are doomed to explain it in a way that others won’t comprehend or find valuable.
When a leader truly understands an idea or problem and can emphasize what is at the heart of the issue, complexity melts away and is replaced by something more elegant.
Anyone can take a complex idea and explain it in a more complex way.
Leaders who prefer to hide behind complex explanations and obtuse language do so to project a sophisticated self-image that falls flat.
The mark of a great mind is an ability to take what few can truly understand and make it clear and actionable.
